statement: Selection of all cryptographic algorithms is deferred to a dedicated security review; only the cryptographic architecture is decided in §9.
research_needed: External cryptographic security review selecting AEAD, KDF, hash, KEM, signature and password-KDF instantiations
decision_needed: Which concrete primitives instantiate the v1 PayloadSuite, recipient KEMs, signature scheme and password KDF?

statement: The encryption, authentication and signature architecture (envelope, commitment, segment keying, signature bindings, agility rules) is decided in the architecture document, independent of algorithm choice.
research_needed: Formal analysis that the architecture is sound independent of instantiation (§25.2)

statement: Legacy ZIP encryption (ZipCrypto) is unauthenticated and cryptographically broken.
research_needed: Primary citation (known-plaintext attack literature) and check of current ZIP tooling defaults

statement: ZIP AES uses AES-CTR with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 at 1000 iterations and only a truncated 80-bit HMAC over entry data that never covers the central directory.
research_needed: Verify against WinZip AE-1/AE-2 specification and current implementations (7-Zip, libzip, Info-ZIP)

statement: 7z encryption is AES-256-CBC with iterated SHA-256 KDF and no authentication; integrity is unkeyed CRC32 an attacker can recompute after modifying ciphertext.
research_needed: Verify against 7z format documentation and current 7-Zip source; demonstrate ciphertext malleability

statement: RAR5 uses AES-256-CBC with PBKDF2 and has no MAC; its key-dependent tweaked checksums block content guessing but are not authentication.
research_needed: Verify against RAR5 technote and unrar source; check whether RAR 7.x changed this

statement: Every incumbent archive format fails the authenticated-encryption baseline (ZIP legacy, ZIP AES, 7z, RAR5 listed).
evidence_in_source: table of four formats, no citations
research_needed: Survey broader incumbents (age+tar, zstd with external crypto, borg/restic, DAR, WIM, squashfs) before publishing a universal claim

statement: Authenticated encryption always: there is no configuration or mode in which an Entrybound archive is encrypted but unauthenticated.
research_needed: Conformance tests proving no writer or reader path accepts unauthenticated ciphertext

statement: Cryptographic choices are decomposed into three orthogonal axes (PayloadSuite, RecipientMethod, SignatureMethod) rather than a combinatorial ciphersuite matrix.
evidence_in_source: analogy to modern transport security and an encrypted-archive format's profile numbering

statement: PayloadSuite (payload AEAD, KDF and hash) is exactly one per format version and never negotiated; a second payload suite means a second format version.
RecipientMethod (how the file key is wrapped) is extensible and an archive may carry multiple recipient methods.
SignatureMethod (how authorship is asserted) is extensible, optional, and an archive may carry multiple signatures.
decision_needed: How are unknown SignatureMethod types handled by a verifier (ignored, reported, refused)?

statement: The three-axis decomposition is what tamed ciphersuite explosion in modern transport security and matches a shipping encrypted-archive format's profile numbering that makes signing and encryption orthogonal.
research_needed: Name and cite the shipping format and TLS 1.3 design rationale

statement: Unbounded algorithm agility accretes over decades and ends in governance schism, as demonstrated by the OpenPGP ecosystem's unresolved fork.
evidence_in_source: uncited reference to OpenPGP (RFC 9580 vs LibrePGP) split
research_needed: Primary citation of the OpenPGP/LibrePGP divergence

statement: CryptoEnvelope contains suite_id (fixed by format version), commitment (§9.4), a list of recipient stanzas (one per recipient), and envelope_mac over the whole envelope.
decision_needed: What is the exact byte encoding of the envelope and stanza framing?

statement: suite_id is fixed by format version yet stored separately; the source does not say how a reader treats a suite_id that disagrees with the format version, or whether this restates one fact twice.
research_needed: Spec consistency review against I19 and agility rule 5
decision_needed: Is suite_id a validated redundant field bound into KDF context, or derived from the version and not stored?

statement: envelope_mac authenticates the entire envelope and is keyed from the file key.
research_needed: Formal analysis of MAC key derivation separation from payload key and commitment

statement: A random file key is generated per archive; the payload is encrypted exactly once regardless of recipient count.
Each RecipientStanza independently wraps the file key; stanza types are the format's cryptographic extensibility seam.
Readers ignore unknown stanza types, but the envelope MAC covers all stanzas, so stanza injection, removal or mutation is detected.
research_needed: Security analysis of the ignore-but-authenticate rule, including attacker-crafted unknown stanzas and parser DoS

statement: The stanza design is adopted from a modern file-encryption format that shipped post-quantum recipients in a point release without a format version bump.
research_needed: Cite the age release and specification that added hybrid PQ recipients

statement: Adding a recipient is appending a stanza; because the envelope MAC is keyed from the file key, only a party able to decrypt can add a recipient.
Removing a recipient requires re-encryption; the specification must state that removal revokes only future access, never copies already read, since past readers hold the file key.
The `entrybound key remove` command performs a re-encryption and explicitly tells the user it does so.

Because the envelope MAC is keyed from the file key, any legitimate recipient can add, remove or alter stanzas and recompute the MAC; insider-recipient envelope tampering is not addressed except via signature addressing bindings.
research_needed: Threat-model analysis with a malicious-recipient adversary; decide whether unsigned encrypted archives need sender authentication
decision_needed: Is recipient-set integrity against other recipients a v1 goal, or only against outsiders?

statement: Contradiction: §9.3 makes adding a recipient a stanza append with the same file key, but §9.6 says key add invalidates the physical binding on encrypted archives because boundaries are key-derived, implying re-encryption.
research_needed: Spec reconciliation
decision_needed: Does `key add` preserve the file key and chunk boundaries (physical binding stays valid) or re-encrypt?

statement: Recipient removal re-encrypts with a new file key, which re-derives key-dependent chunk boundaries; the cost (full re-chunk, recompression, rewrite) and whether it can avoid recompressing is not stated.
research_needed: Measure re-encryption cost on large archives; explore whether boundary secrets can be separated from the file key
decision_needed: Should boundary-derivation secrets survive recipient removal?

statement: Recipient key management is unspecified: recipient identifier formats, key files, SSH keys, hardware tokens or plugins, and how a user names recipients.
research_needed: Usability study and survey of age/minisign/sigstore recipient UX
decision_needed: Which recipient key formats and plugin mechanisms does v1 support?

statement: One KDF invocation over the file key yields payload_key, base_nonce and commitment together.
research_needed: Formal analysis of the key-derivation hierarchy and commitment (§25.2 L2562)

statement: The commitment is stored in the envelope and verified before any payload byte is decrypted.
research_needed: Conformance tests that no plaintext is released before commitment check

statement: Common AEADs are not key-committing; published attacks build one ciphertext that decrypts validly under two keys, directly exploitable in multi-recipient archives so two recipients see different content.
research_needed: Cite partitioning-oracle / invisible-salamanders literature; demonstrate attack against a non-committing multi-recipient construction

statement: Three independent systems (a major cloud provider's encryption SDK and two community specifications) derive commitment from the KDF, at a cost of about 32 bytes.
research_needed: Name and cite the three systems; confirm 32-byte commitment gives the targeted collision resistance

statement: There is no IETF or IRTF work item for a committing AEAD, so waiting for a standardized one is not viable.
research_needed: Re-check CFRG/IETF status as of 2026 (AEAD properties and committing-AEAD drafts)

statement: Key commitment is obtained from the construction, not from the AEAD primitive, making it algorithm-agnostic and compatible with the agility rules of §9.9.
Random nonces with a 96-bit-nonce AEAD are unsafe for archives with tens of millions of chunks.
research_needed: Quantify nonce-collision probability and AEAD usage limits per key at 10^7-10^9 chunks for candidate AEADs

statement: A single global nonce counter across machines is an operational hazard: one deployed backup system reserves counter ranges locally and in the repository and warns a hostile repository can force counter reuse.
evidence_in_source: uncited reference to a backup system's documentation
research_needed: Cite the borg documentation on nonce reservation

statement: A Segment is a first-class model object: the unit of key derivation and nonce counting.
refines_or_supersedes: Fixes changelog item L2647 (Segment previously absent from model); listed in §3.1 object list L134

statement: Segment has segment_id (monotonic within the archive), a contiguous range of the archive's chunk sequence, and a random per-segment salt stored in the manifest.
Segments must be sized so a segment's nonce counter cannot approach its AEAD's message limit.
research_needed: Derive the maximum chunks-per-segment from the chosen AEAD's usage limits
decision_needed: What is the maximum segment size, and is it a format constant or writer-chosen?

statement: Segment sizing policy is unspecified: fixed format constant or planner/writer choice, and whether segmentation affects deterministic output and PCR.
research_needed: Measure impact of segment size on range-read key derivation cost and re-encryption
decision_needed: Who chooses segment boundaries and are they part of deterministic-mode output?

statement: Every chunk belongs to exactly one segment, declared once by the segment's range and never by a per-chunk field (I19).
The chunk table maps a chunk index to its segment in O(1), so a range-reading client derives exactly the segment keys it needs.
O(1) chunk-to-segment mapping without any per-chunk field implies fixed-size segments or an auxiliary table; variable-length contiguous ranges give logarithmic lookup. The mechanism is unstated.
decision_needed: Are segments uniformly sized (arithmetic mapping) or is O(1) relaxed to O(log n)?

statement: Segment salts are said to live in the manifest while segments also appear in the CRYPTO_ENVELOPE section; if the manifest is encrypted, how the manifest's own key/nonce is bootstrapped and where salts are readable is not specified.
research_needed: Specify the key schedule for manifest, index and payload sections
decision_needed: Where are segment descriptors stored, and which key protects the manifest itself?

statement: A range reader detects segment truncation by validating the segment's declared first and last chunk indices against the chunk table before deriving any key.
A sequential reader detects truncation via a final-chunk marker in the last chunk's nonce derivation.
Two-level keying: a per-segment key is derived from the file key and the segment's random salt.
Within a segment, nonces are a pure counter.
The segment identifier is bound into the per-chunk key/nonce derivation.
Final marker, monotonic counter and segment binding together defeat truncation, reordering and cross-archive chunk splicing.
refines_or_supersedes: Routed to formal analysis in §25.2 L2562
research_needed: Formal proof or model-checking of the segment construction

statement: Per-segment final markers detect a truncated segment, but removal of whole trailing segments (or of the segment list tail) is not explicitly covered; segment count must be authenticated somewhere.
research_needed: Security review of whole-segment deletion and segment-range rewriting attacks
decision_needed: Which authenticated structure binds the total segment count?

statement: A file-encryption format, the next major version of a deployed backup tool and a community chunked-encryption spec independently converged on this keying shape, which is presented as strong evidence of correctness.
research_needed: Cite the three designs and compare details (salt placement, marker, id binding)

statement: Signatures are over root descriptors, never over the payload bytes and never over container bytes.
Residual inconsistency: the text still says there are two signature scopes, while the defined structure is one signature with three bindings.
refines_or_supersedes: Changelog L2630 (two scopes) superseded by L2669 (three bindings)
research_needed: Editorial correction

statement: A signature object is a single signature carrying three independent bindings, each verified and reported separately.
content_binding contains LAI, AUX, identity_profile_id and format_version, and is always present.
physical_binding contains PCR and is optional; it lets a verifier check a byte range against a signed root.
addressing_binding contains payload_suite_id, recipient_set_digest and commitment, and is optional.

How one signature over three bindings lets a verifier report content VALID while physical is STALE is unspecified: signed-structure encoding, whether stale binding values are retained, and whether bindings can be omitted after signing.
research_needed: Formal specification of the signed transcript and domain separation; cross-context confusion analysis (§25.2 L2564)
decision_needed: What exact byte structure is signed, and how are optional bindings represented?

statement: recipient_set_digest is undefined: over stanza bytes (including unknown and padding stanzas) or recipient identities, and how password recipients and optional stanza padding affect it.
decision_needed: What canonical input does recipient_set_digest hash?

statement: content_binding is invalidated by content change, entry-set change, metadata change or provenance strip; physical_binding by re-chunking, re-encryption or profile change; addressing_binding by any recipient-set change.
Signature verification reports each binding separately with statuses such as VALID, STALE and ABSENT; a stale physical binding falls back to the archive's own unsigned PCR for range verification.
The source does not define how a verifier distinguishes STALE (legitimately re-chunked) from INVALID (tampered) physical bindings, nor the full status vocabulary.
refines_or_supersedes: Changelog L2669 says stale is distinguished from invalid
research_needed: Specify detection logic; usability test of verifier output
decision_needed: What evidence makes a binding STALE rather than INVALID, and what are all reportable states?

statement: The binding split is forced: anti-forwarding must break on audience change, physical binding on chunking change, while content binding must survive both or migration becomes a re-signing event as in incumbents.
refines_or_supersedes: Corrects an earlier draft that put all three in one binding
research_needed: Security review of composition (§25.2 L2564)

statement: Default bindings: unencrypted archives get content and physical bindings; encrypted archives get all three.
The addressing binding must not survive re-encryption or any audience change; this breakage is correct behaviour for anti-forwarding.
refines_or_supersedes: Corrects earlier draft claiming both recipient binding and survival of re-encryption

statement: `key add` and `key remove` invalidate the addressing binding and, on encrypted archives, the physical binding, leaving the content binding valid.
`repack --profile` invalidates only the physical binding; `repack --strip-provenance` invalidates the content binding because AUX is inside it.
Every command that alters an archive reports exactly which signature bindings it will invalidate before doing anything.

Naive sign-then-encrypt and encrypt-then-sign both permit surreptitious forwarding across many mail and document standards; the classic analysis says the fix is binding the inner layer to the outer, not ordering.
research_needed: Cite the analysis and verify the recipient-set binding achieves its stated fix

statement: Entrybound signs then encrypts, hiding signature and author identity from ciphertext observers, and names the recipient set in the addressing binding.

Detached signatures on encrypted archives would expose signer identity and signed roots (LAI, commitment) to anyone, contradicting the signer-hiding rationale; LAI exposure may enable confirmation-of-file. Handling is unspecified.
research_needed: Privacy analysis of publishing LAI/AUX for encrypted content
decision_needed: Are detached signatures permitted for encrypted archives, and must signed roots be keyed or hidden?

statement: Detached and embedded signatures are byte-identical over the same canonical signed object.

Detached signing must allow signing a deterministic archive without changing its bytes and allow multiple parties to sign independently without nesting; embedded signing must survive transports that drop sidecars.
Trusted timestamps on signatures are supported and recommended, because an archive outlives its signing certificate.
The trusted-timestamp protocol, what is timestamped (signature bytes or roots), and how timestamp tokens are verified offline decades later are unspecified.
research_needed: Evaluate RFC 3161 and alternatives for offline long-term verification
decision_needed: Which timestamp token format is built in and over which bytes?

statement: Signer trust semantics are not specified: key identifiers, certificates or bare keys, trust stores, and what 'signed by release-key' asserts to a user.
research_needed: Usability and security review of signer identity presentation
decision_needed: What trust model and signer-identity representation does v1 verification use?

statement: Attestations are a separate additive layer carried as signature-set members keyed to the LAI, so existing supply-chain attestation ecosystems attach without translation.
Entrybound does not invent its own provenance or attestation format.

Verification must never depend on live infrastructure; keyless signing requiring a live CA, identity provider and transparency log is only an optional sidecar, and the built-in path is a self-contained signature plus optional timestamp.
Which attestation envelope formats are carried, how 'keyed to the LAI' behaves when only AUX changes, and whether keyless-signing sidecars are members of the signature set are unspecified.
decision_needed: Which attestation envelope(s) are supported and bound to which root?

statement: Signature scheme instantiation is deferred; the composition's resistance to surreptitious forwarding and cross-context confusion is routed to security review.
research_needed: Security review of signature composition, context strings and multi-binding verification
decision_needed: Which signature scheme(s) instantiate SignatureMethod in v1?

statement: identity_profile_id in the content binding implies signatures per identity profile; whether one archive may carry signatures under different profiles (identity/v1 vs strict) and how verify reports them is unstated.
decision_needed: Can multiple identity profiles be signed in one archive?

statement: Deduplication over encrypted data is scoped to one key domain; within an archive or key domain dedup is free and safe.
Cross-domain and cross-tenant deduplication over encrypted data, and convergent encryption, are rejected and not offered.
Convergent encryption enables confirmation-of-a-file and learn-the-remaining-information attacks, which are well documented and practical.
research_needed: Primary citations

statement: Server-aided convergent encryption with a rate-limited key oracle is rejected because it requires a live trusted party at every encryption, incompatible with infrastructure-free long-term readability.
Every serious deduplicating backup system scopes dedup to a repository using a secret chunker parameter and keyed chunk identifiers.
research_needed: Survey borg, restic, kopia, duplicacy, bupstash for chunker secrecy and keyed ids

statement: Encrypted archives use a secret chunker parameter and keyed chunk identifiers, like deduplicating backup systems.
refines_or_supersedes: Interacts with §7.6 default chunking vs `--chunk-boundary=keyed-prf` option (L853)
decision_needed: Is a secret chunker parameter on by default for encrypted archives, distinct from the optional keyed-prf mode?

statement: 'Key domain' is not defined: whether it can span several archives (incremental archives, base chains, repositories) and how keyed chunk identifiers and file keys are shared across archives in one domain.
research_needed: Design and security analysis of multi-archive key domains
decision_needed: What constitutes a key domain and can it exceed one archive in v1?

statement: In an encrypted archive, filenames and directory structure are hidden by default at approximately zero cost via the encrypted manifest.
Entry count is hidden by default in encrypted archives, at the cost of index padding.
decision_needed: What index/manifest padding schedule hides entry count, and is it on by default?

statement: Per-entry sizes, metadata and the fidelity report are hidden by default inside the encrypted manifest at approximately zero cost.
Total archive size is not hidden and cannot be.
Recipient count is not hidden by default; optional stanza padding may hide it.
decision_needed: What is the stanza padding mechanism and how does it interact with unknown-stanza and recipient-mixing rules?

statement: A password recipient's public commitment is an offline password-verification oracle; this is accepted as the inherent cost of committing constructions and justifies expensive KDF parameters.
research_needed: Security review of whether the stanza wrap already forms the oracle and of acceptable KDF cost

statement: Chunk-size sequence is quantised, not hidden, by bucketed padding (§7.6); `--chunk-boundary=keyed-prf` offers the provably-secure construction.
refines_or_supersedes: Downgraded from 'hidden' per changelog L2645; §4 L468 says 'unless padding is enabled' while §25.1 item 13 says bucketed by default
research_needed: Measured effectiveness of padding schedule against 2025 chunking attacks (§25.2 L2563)
decision_needed: What is the bucket schedule (§25.1 item 13) and is padding on by default?

statement: The keyed-prf chunk-boundary option costs 50-160% in chunking cost; padding carries a declared storage overhead.
research_needed: Benchmark keyed-prf chunking throughput and padding overhead on representative corpora

statement: Hiding access patterns during remote reads is out of scope (would require ORAM-class techniques).
Per-entry size hiding is nearly free for an archive but expensive for encrypted filesystems; one filesystem project documents identifying a music album from per-file sizes.
research_needed: Cite the filesystem documentation (e.g., cryfs/gocryptfs threat model)

statement: Per-entry sizes are claimed hidden, yet quantised chunk sizes and chunk counts (especially one-chunk small files in STREAM order) still leak approximate per-entry sizes; the table does not reconcile these rows.
research_needed: Leakage analysis of file-size recoverability from padded chunk sequences
decision_needed: Should the per-entry size row be downgraded to 'quantised'?

statement: Leakage table omits: encrypted manifest/index lengths, compressed chunk lengths revealing compressibility, plaintext preamble/feature bits/profile/signature presence, dedup ratio, and segment count.
research_needed: Complete leakage inventory in the security review threat model (§25.2 L2565)
decision_needed: Which container fields remain plaintext in an encrypted archive?

statement: §9 states no named adversary model; the threat model with snapshot, persistent read-write and partial-plaintext adversaries is deferred.
research_needed: Threat model documentation with named adversary set
decision_needed: Which adversaries does v1 encryption defend against?

statement: Agility rule 1: one cryptographic suite per format version; a second option is a second version.
Agility rule 2: format version is checked first, at a fixed position, before anything else is parsed; unknown version is rejected with no fallback.
Agility rule 3: orthogonal choices are decomposed (§9.2) rather than enumerated as a combinatorial matrix.
Agility rule 4: cryptographic extensibility is confined to one guarded seam, the recipient stanza, where unknown entries are ignored but authenticated.

Rule 4 names the recipient stanza as the only extensibility seam, but §9.2 also makes SignatureMethod extensible; whether signature methods are a second seam and how unknown ones are treated is unresolved.
decision_needed: Is SignatureMethod an additional guarded seam, and what are its unknown-type rules?

statement: Agility rule 5: an in-band identifier never selects the key type; identifiers are bound into the KDF context and signed transcript so rewriting them fails verification.

A token format's library verified an asymmetric signature using the public key as an HMAC secret after an algorithm-name swap; root cause was attacker-controlled identifier selection, not multiple algorithms.
research_needed: Cite JWT alg-confusion CVEs

statement: Agility rule 6: the deprecation mechanism must be written into v1 because files outlive software (§20.4).
Agility rule 7: version and suite identifiers are signed, not just the payload digest (§9.6).
payload_suite_id is signed only inside the optional addressing binding; an encrypted archive signed without it would leave the suite identifier unsigned, apparently breaking rule 7.
decision_needed: Must payload_suite_id move into the always-present content binding, or is addressing binding mandatory for encrypted archives?

statement: Hybrid post-quantum key encapsulation is mandatory from v1.
Post-quantum signatures are not required in v1; future forgery risk is addressed by re-signing.
Confidentiality is retroactively breakable via harvest-now-decrypt-later; national-standards guidance deprecates classical key establishment on a path ending in the 2030s.
research_needed: Cite NIST IR 8547 / CNSA 2.0 timelines

statement: Signatures made today are not retroactively broken; the standard for the most compact post-quantum signature scheme has not been published.
research_needed: Re-check FN-DSA (FIPS 206) publication status as of 2026

statement: Re-signing as the remedy for future forgery is not operationalised: how distributed archives and detached signatures are re-signed and how timestamps preserve validity of pre-break signatures.
decision_needed: What is the re-signing workflow and does it require rewriting archive bytes?

statement: Deployed consensus on the hybrid is an elliptic-curve-plus-lattice combination used by TLS at majority-of-traffic scale, hybrid HPKE drafts, messaging PQ extensions and the age-like format.
research_needed: Cite deployment data and drafts; confirm exact combiner (e.g., X-Wing) choice

statement: The concrete hybrid KEM instantiation and combiner are not named; only the elliptic-curve-plus-lattice family is indicated.
research_needed: Security review of hybrid combiner
decision_needed: Which hybrid KEM (and parameter set) is the v1 recipient type?

statement: An archive encrypted to a post-quantum recipient must not also be encrypted to a classical-only recipient; enforced at pack time, since multi-recipient security is the minimum over recipients.
Mixing is enforced at pack time only; whether readers or key add also enforce it, and how a reader classifies PQ status of unknown stanza types, is unspecified.
decision_needed: Must readers and key add refuse mixed PQ/classical recipient sets?

statement: If hybrid PQ KEM is mandatory from v1, it is unclear whether classical-only recipient types may exist at all (e.g., SSH or X25519 keys), or only may not be mixed with PQ recipients.
decision_needed: Does v1 permit any classical-only recipient type?

statement: Password-based access to encrypted archives is supported.
Password KDF parameters are stored as verifiable fields in the archive, not compile-time constants, and `entrybound inspect` reports whether they meet current guidance.
Password KDF parameters target the offline, rare, interactive archive-unlock case and bias toward the higher-cost end of guidance, with the reason stated.
Server-authentication password hashing guidance recommends far lower memory than the memory-hard KDF specification's own recommendation because threat models differ.
research_needed: Cite both guidance documents with parameter values

statement: Password KDF choice and default parameter values are not set in §9.11.
refines_or_supersedes: §25.1 item 12 (L2544); §11 L1397 adds an enforced cost ceiling
research_needed: Benchmark memory-hard KDF on low-end and high-end hardware; choose default and ceiling
decision_needed: What are the default KDF parameters and the maximum accepted cost ceiling?

statement: A password recipient may not be combined with stronger recipient types in the same archive, mirroring an existing format's rule that its password stanza is the only stanza.
refines_or_supersedes: CLI restates at L1855 (--password not combinable with --recipient)

statement: Text announces two deliberate choices but lists three; also unresolved whether multiple password recipients may coexist in one archive.
decision_needed: May an archive have more than one password stanza?

statement: The source of 'current guidance' against which inspect evaluates stored KDF parameters, and how that guidance is updated in a long-lived tool, is unspecified.
decision_needed: What baseline does inspect use and is it versioned with the tool?

statement: MetadataItem has namespace, name, typed value, criticality (Critical or Optional), restore class (Restorable, CaptureOnly, PlatformSpecific) and a fidelity declaration.
Metadata is never a bag of anonymous extra fields: every item is typed, namespaced, and carries its own criticality and restorability (I11).
evidence_in_source: contrast with ZIP extra fields and tar vendor keywords

statement: TypedValue's type system and the FidelityDeclaration structure are not defined in §10.
decision_needed: What value types exist and what does a per-item FidelityDeclaration contain?

statement: Criticality and restore class are per-item fields, yet the registry carries a criticality default and restorability class per name; whether writers may override defaults, or whether storing both restates one fact, is unclear.
decision_needed: Are criticality and restore stored per item or implied by the registry?

statement: ZIP extra fields are designed to be skipped and cannot express must-understand; tar SCHILY.xattr and LIBARCHIVE.xattr keywords are widely implemented but non-normative.
research_needed: Cite APPNOTE and pax/libarchive documentation

statement: Metadata namespaces are core., posix., linux., windows., macos., security., provenance., and x-<domain>. with portability universal, per-platform, cross-platform or by agreement.
core. and the platform namespaces are closed: new names need a format revision and writers may not invent names in a closed namespace.
x- namespaces are open to applications and vendors and MUST use reverse-DNS naming.

§10.2 closes only core. and platform namespaces, but §10.2a enumerates security. and provenance. too and says adding a name to any listed namespace needs a format revision; their open/closed status is ambiguous.
decision_needed: Are security. and provenance. closed namespaces?

statement: Residual contradiction: §10.2 table still lists size, kind and content digest under core., while §10.2a says model fields have no metadata names.
refines_or_supersedes: Changelog L2676 claims the restatement was fixed
research_needed: Editorial correction of §10.2 table

statement: Table and enumeration disagree: capabilities under posix. vs linux.; table omits id_space, atime/ctime/btime, sparse_hint, device numbers, case_sensitive_dir and signature_state.
research_needed: Editorial reconciliation

statement: Handling of x- items is underspecified: whether reverse-DNS validity is checked, whether any registry exists, and whether a Critical x- item forces refusal by all other readers.
decision_needed: May x- items be Critical, and how are malformed x- names handled?

statement: The POSIX archive standard reserves all-lowercase keywords for future standardisation and pushes vendors to prefixed names; Entrybound makes this structural rather than advisory.
research_needed: Cite POSIX pax keyword rules

statement: The v1 membership of the closed metadata namespaces is fixed by the enumeration in §10.2a.
The registry (§20.3) records for each metadata name its type, criticality default, restorability class, and whether it participates in identity/v1.

Registry records identity/v1 participation only, but identity/strict-v1 includes full mode bits, ownership names, mtime and hardlink_group; per-profile participation is not represented in the registry.
decision_needed: Does the registry carry participation per identity profile?

statement: Metadata never restates a model field: path, kind, encoding, content digest, chunk list and symlink target have no metadata names (E1, I19).
core. contains exactly executable (the only identity/v1 participant) and mtime.

posix. contains mode, uid, gid, uname, gname, id_space, atime, ctime, btime, POSIX access/default ACLs, NFSv4 ACL, repeatable name-keyed xattr, hardlink_group, sparse_hint, device_major and device_minor.
linux. contains selinux_label, capability (with revision and namespace root ID), and statx_attributes.
windows. contains file_attributes, binary self-relative security_descriptor, repeatable alternate_stream, reparse_data, creation_time, zone_identifier and case_sensitive_dir.
macos. contains resource_fork, finder_info (exactly 32 bytes), acl_macos, quarantine, provenance, decmpfs (opaque, capture-only) and uf_flags.
security. contains origin_url, origin_referrer and signature_state.
provenance. contains source_format, source_digest, import_mode, import_runtime and tool_version.
Adding a name to any enumerated namespace is a format revision with a feature bit, never a writer decision.

windows.alternate_stream and macos.resource_fork are metadata items; whether their payloads are inline metadata values (bounded how) or ContentObjects with chunking, dedup, random access and extraction confinement is unspecified.
research_needed: Survey real-world ADS/resource fork sizes; security review of fork restoration
decision_needed: Are fork/stream payloads stored as content objects referenced from metadata, or inline values?

statement: Several names can carry the same fact: posix.btime vs windows.creation_time; windows.zone_identifier or macos.quarantine vs security.origin_url; ownership in posix.uid vs windows.security_descriptor. Authority and dedup rules are unspecified.
decision_needed: Which name is authoritative when platform and cross-platform names overlap?

statement: security.signature_state is undefined (OS code-signing state, Authenticode, or Entrybound signature state); if the latter, recording it inside AUX would be circular with signatures over AUX.
decision_needed: What does security.signature_state record?

statement: Many named items are xattrs on their platform (SELinux label, file capability, macOS quarantine/provenance/FinderInfo/resource fork/decmpfs); rules preventing the same bytes being captured both as posix.xattr and as the named item are absent.
decision_needed: Which xattr names are excluded from posix.xattr because a dedicated name exists?

statement: Closed-namespace coverage may be incomplete: e.g., Windows 8.3 short names, object IDs, EFS state; Linux chattr flags; BSD chflags; macOS tags; illumos ACLs. Such facts cannot be written without a format revision.
research_needed: Platform metadata survey against incumbent preservation (tar/pax, WIM, dar, ditto)
decision_needed: Which additional closed names must v1 include?

statement: device_major/device_minor widths and encodings across Linux, BSD and macOS (different dev_t splits) are unspecified.
decision_needed: How are device numbers encoded portably?

statement: A reader that does not understand a Critical metadata item must refuse the entry, and at the archive's option the whole archive; Critical is reserved for items whose absence changes an entry's meaning.
evidence_in_source: precedent: PNG chunks, X.509 extensions, OpenPGP subpackets

statement: How an archive expresses its option to refuse the whole archive on an unknown critical item, which v1 names default to Critical, and what 'understand' means for a known name with an unknown value are unspecified.
decision_needed: Where is the archive-wide refusal option encoded, and which registry names are Critical by default?

statement: Optional items may be ignored by readers but are covered by the entry's identity_digest or aux_digest, and therefore by the content binding, so they cannot be silently altered.
refines_or_supersedes: §8.0 L885 (every metadata byte under LAI or AUX)

statement: Contradiction: every Optional item is said to be covered by identity or AUX digests, but posix.sparse_hint participates in no digest, so it is unauthenticated and alterable in a signed archive.
refines_or_supersedes: Also conflicts with §8.0 L885; changelog L2632 excluded sparse map everywhere
decision_needed: Is sparse_hint covered by AUX (but not identity), or is it an explicit unauthenticated exception?

statement: Per-element criticality bits complement, not replace, the archive-level three-tier feature bitmap (§20.1), which expresses read-but-not-write.
refines_or_supersedes: §20.1 L2166; §20.1 L2184 notes a critical-name list alternative if encoding lacks a bit
evidence_in_source: precedent from image, certificate and signature formats

statement: Write-side behaviour for unknown items is unstated: whether repack or a writer must preserve, drop, or refuse unknown Critical and Optional items.
decision_needed: What must a writer do with metadata items it does not understand?

statement: Timestamps are signed 64-bit seconds plus unsigned 32-bit nanoseconds, never floating point; these widths are fixed in the architecture as a semantic decision.
refines_or_supersedes: Narrows §25.1 item 2 (L2534) which otherwise defers field widths

statement: Each timestamp records source precision (Second, Centisecond, Microsecond, Hectonanosecond, Nanosecond), preventing spurious diffs and invented precision on round trip.
The precision enumeration lacks two-second (FAT/ZIP DOS time), millisecond and unknown precisions needed for legacy and cross-platform sources.
research_needed: Survey timestamp precision across filesystems and legacy formats (FAT, exFAT, HFS+, ZIP, tar, 7z, NTFS, SMB/NFS)
decision_needed: Which precision values does the enum include?

statement: Timestamp semantics are incomplete: epoch and time scale (UTC, leap seconds), handling of zone-less local times from legacy formats, nanosecond validity range and canonical form for negative seconds.
decision_needed: What epoch, time scale and canonical validity rules apply to Timestamp?

statement: Restorability is recorded per timestamp, so a captured but unrestorable time (e.g., Linux birth time) is declared rather than dropped or falsely restored.
Per-timestamp restorable bool overlaps with the MetadataItem restore class, and restorability depends on the extraction target, so what an archive-time bool asserts is unclear.
decision_needed: Is timestamp restorability a source-side declaration, target-evaluated at extraction, or removed in favour of restore class?

statement: Timestamp fidelity is a per-filesystem property recorded per archive, not assumed from the platform.

Platform timestamp limits: ext4 128-byte inodes have 32-bit seconds, no creation time and a 2038 cliff; larger inodes give 34-bit seconds with nanoseconds to 2446; another filesystem extends to 2486; Windows uses 1601 epoch with 100ns units.
evidence_in_source: presented as measured platform reality; no citations
research_needed: Cite kernel/filesystem documentation for each limit

statement: No Linux system call sets file birth time, so it can be recorded but never restored.
research_needed: Verify against current Linux kernel APIs as of 2026

statement: Classic tar's fixed-width octal timestamp expires in 2242 and lacks access and creation times, while pax decimal-string extended headers are unbounded in range and precision.
research_needed: Verify octal field arithmetic and pax spec

statement: Ownership is a tagged union of Posix {uid, gid, optional uname and gname, id_space} and Windows {owner_sid, group_sid}, because no lossless mapping exists.
Both numeric IDs and names are carried, with names preferred when resolvable, following the POSIX archive standard's model.
id_space records which ID space a numeric owner came from, because with ID-mapped mounts the observed owner is a view and restore in different namespaces yields different on-disk owners.
evidence_in_source: reference to kernel documentation (three ID spaces)

statement: id_space value domain and capture feasibility are unspecified: what values exist, and how an unprivileged safe-Rust archiver detects ID-mapped mounts and its user-namespace mapping.
research_needed: Prototype detection of idmapped mounts and userns mappings via Linux APIs
decision_needed: What values can id_space take?

statement: No incumbent archive format records an ID-space field, and every container user needs it.
research_needed: Survey OCI layers, tar variants, squashfs, WIM and container user needs

statement: Cross-platform ownership restore is an extractor policy decision, not a representable value; the extraction report records what happened.

Ownership.Windows {owner_sid, group_sid} has no matching names in the closed windows. namespace (only security_descriptor), so it is unclear whether SIDs are separate fields or derived from the descriptor.
decision_needed: Where are Windows owner/group SIDs stored, and is Ownership a model field or metadata?

statement: Entrybound does not convert between permission models (POSIX mode, POSIX ACLs, NFSv4 ACLs, Windows security descriptors, macOS ACLs); any conversion is an export-adapter policy with a receipt, never part of the model.
Editorial inconsistency: text says four distinct permission types but lists five.
research_needed: Editorial correction

statement: Restore order is normative: ACLs are applied last, after permission bits, because chmod and ACL mask interact.
On POSIX-ACL filesystems, changing mode bits changes ACL entries and vice versa; with a mask, group bits are the mask, so chmod-then-setfacl and setfacl-then-chmod yield different files.
research_needed: Test on ext4/xfs/btrfs with and without mask entries

statement: Windows security descriptors are stored in binary self-relative form; the text (SDDL) form is only a human-readable annotation.
The security descriptor text form has separate grammar for conditional entries and resource attributes and does not round-trip reliably.
research_needed: Round-trip test of SDDL conversion APIs

statement: Only ACL-last ordering is fixed; order relative to ownership changes (which clear setuid and capabilities), xattrs, immutable flags, SELinux labels, Windows attributes/SDs and final timestamp setting is unspecified, as is ACL inheritance on targets.
research_needed: Platform experiments determining a safe total restore order per OS
decision_needed: What is the complete normative metadata restore order per platform?

statement: Extended attributes are stored with exact name bytes, value bytes and namespace.

Kernel xattr limits are 255-byte names and 64 KiB values, but the most common Linux filesystem requires all of a file's xattrs to fit in one 1-4 KiB block, so a 64 KiB attribute cannot be restored there.
research_needed: Verify ext4 limits including the ea_inode feature which allows large values; measure per-filesystem limits

statement: Archives record per-attribute sizes and a total xattr budget, and extraction surfaces unrepresentable-on-target attributes during planning, not mid-extraction.
Extraction planning must know target filesystem xattr limits in advance, but no portable API reports them (e.g., ext4 block size and ea_inode); how planning determines limits is unspecified.
research_needed: Prototype target-capability probing on Linux/macOS/Windows in safe Rust
decision_needed: Does planning probe, assume, or learn limits at runtime?

statement: Linux namespaced file capabilities, whose root ID is meaningful in one user namespace, are marked PlatformSpecific with the namespace recorded.
The macOS filesystem-compression attribute is CaptureOnly opaque data and is never synthesised.
The macOS filesystem-compression attribute has no published specification.
research_needed: Check Apple documentation and open-source xnu headers

statement: There is no sparse-map structure: a hole is a chunk, and the source filesystem's hole geometry is only a metadata hint.
Holes add no separately parsed map; the existing chunk-count budget (I20) bounds them with no special case.
A 2026 memory-exhaustion vulnerability in a major language's tar reader came from header-resident chain-extended sparse maps; its fix capped extension blocks and total entry count.
research_needed: Cite the CVE and fix details

statement: A hole chunk's logical_len equals the zero bytes it produces and the sum of logical_len is the content size; no second size term can diverge.
posix.sparse_hint records what the source reported and participates in no digest, no identity and no size.
refines_or_supersedes: Consistent with §8 L953; conflicts with §10.3 L1246

statement: Filesystems need not report holes accurately, every file has an implicit end hole, a mainstream extractor invents sparseness by scanning zero runs, and two faithful archivers can produce different geometries for identical files.
research_needed: Test SEEK_HOLE/FSCTL_QUERY_ALLOCATED_RANGES accuracy; identify the extractor

statement: Sparse restoration is extraction policy, defaulting to restoring holes where the target supports them and otherwise writing zeros, with the outcome reported.

Hole-chunk mechanics are unspecified: whether one hole chunk may exceed CDC max chunk size (else a terabyte hole consumes huge chunk counts), how holes are detected at pack time, and whether detection affects deterministic output and PCR.
research_needed: Measure chunk counts and pack time for large sparse files (VM images, databases)
decision_needed: Are hole chunks exempt from max chunk size, and is hole detection by zero-run or filesystem query?

statement: Whether extraction restores holes from hole chunks or from the unauthenticated sparse_hint is not stated; if the hint drives restoration, tampering could alter on-disk allocation.
decision_needed: Which input drives hole restoration?

statement: The archive stores exact filename bytes plus a declared encoding and does not normalise names.
Name-collision detection is a normative obligation of the extractor (P5).

The two most widely used filesystems disagree: one stores a normalised form on disk; its successor preserves caller form while hashing a normalised form; they use different Unicode versions, so round-tripping is not identity.
research_needed: Cite Apple documentation and test round trips across HFS+/APFS

statement: Extractor collision detection needs the target's normalisation and case-folding rules (Unicode version, per-directory case sensitivity on NTFS or ext4 casefold); how these are determined at extraction time is unspecified.
research_needed: Prototype per-directory case/normalisation probing on Windows, macOS, Linux
decision_needed: Does the extractor probe the target, apply a conservative superset rule, or both?

statement: Every archive carries a FIDELITY section.
Every extraction produces a FidelityReport of the same structure as output.

FidelityReport contains captured metadata classes, unavailable {class, reason, entry_scope}, degraded {class, from, to, entry_scope}, source platform description, and per-filesystem {mount, timestamp precision, xattr limits, ACL model, case sensitivity}.
MetadataClass vocabulary, reason codes, entry_scope encoding (potentially unbounded lists, I20), and SourcePlatformDescription content are undefined.
decision_needed: How are fidelity classes, reasons and entry scopes encoded and bounded?

statement: The report must be able to record items such as unrestorable birth time, ACL presence counts, xattrs exceeding ext4 limits, case-insensitive source with collision pairs, and missing privilege to read trusted. xattrs.
The FidelityReport is in-band and typed, not a log; it is covered by the AUX digest and any signature, and queryable via `entrybound inspect --fidelity`.
The FidelityReport does not participate in LAI, so re-importing a source with a newer tool leaves the identity of unchanged content unchanged.
A FidelityReport cannot be stripped from a signed archive without invalidating the signature, giving the no-silent-loss guarantee (I13) cryptographic backing.

Platform description and mount paths in the report make AUX host-dependent: packing identical trees on two machines yields different AUX and signed content, and unencrypted archives disclose host details. Redaction or deterministic options are unspecified.
research_needed: Evaluate reproducible-build impact and privacy exposure of fidelity report fields
decision_needed: Should deterministic mode normalise or omit host-specific fidelity fields?

statement: Where and how the extraction-time FidelityReport is emitted (stdout, file, API), whether it is persisted or signed, and its relation to the §11 extraction report and conversion receipts are unspecified.
decision_needed: What is the output channel and format of extraction fidelity reports?

statement: No existing format addresses declared per-archive fidelity loss; the report implements philosophy statement (5) by making every platform loss a first-class record.
research_needed: Survey incumbents (pax, WIM, dar, mtree, bsdtar warnings) for comparable fidelity declarations
